Using the standard notation

\[
[X/Y]=\log_{10}\frac{(n_X/n_Y)_\star}{(n_X/n_Y)_\odot},
\]

we can combine abundance ratios:

### Star 1

\[
[\mathrm{Si/H}]_1=[\mathrm{Si/Fe}]_1+[\mathrm{Fe/H}]_1
=0.3+0=0.3.
\]

Thus,

\[
\left(\frac{n_{\rm Si}}{n_{\rm H}}\right)_1
=10^{0.3}\left(\frac{n_{\rm Si}}{n_{\rm H}}\right)_\odot.
\]

### Star 2

Since

\[
[\mathrm{Mg/Si}]_2=[\mathrm{Mg/H}]_2-[\mathrm{Si/H}]_2,
\]

\[
0.3=0-[\mathrm{Si/H}]_2,
\]

so

\[
[\mathrm{Si/H}]_2=-0.3.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{(n_{\rm Si}/n_{\rm H})_1}{(n_{\rm Si}/n_{\rm H})_2}
=10^{0.3-(-0.3)}
=10^{0.6}
\approx 3.98\approx 3.9.
\]

The solar Fe and Mg abundances cancel through the common solar silicon reference, and the stellar masses are irrelevant to this abundance ratio.

Answer: D
